Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

CANNES, France (CNN) -- After eleven days, hundreds of screenings and thousands of snaps from the paparazzi, there could only be one Palme d'Or winner. Austrian director Michael Haneke hugs the president of the Cannes jury, French actress Isabelle Huppert. "The White Ribbon," by Austrian director Michael Haneke, was awarded the prize for its depiction of the cruel punishments meted out at a rural German school before the First World War. "The Palme d'Or is the best prize a filmmaker can win," said Haneke at a press conference following his award. "I am not proud, but I am very happy. In my opinion, it's silly to be proud." It was a case of fifth time lucky for Haneke, who has previously been nominated for the award for "Funny Games" (1997), "Code Unknown" (2000), "The Piano Teacher" (2001) and "Hidden" (2005). "There are always rumors at the festival, and one must not take them seriously," the director said. "When I presented "Hidden" [in 2005], everyone was telling me I was going to win the Palme. And I didn't get it." Jury president Isabelle Huppert, the French actress who won the best actress prize at the 2001 festival for "The Piano Teacher," said she was delighted to have the chance to honor her former director. "I think I always loved him as a director, and that's why I've worked with him before," she said at the post-awards press conference. "To me, the movie is very philosophical. And his style, and his direction are totally ethical in my mind. That's what I wanted to reward." The American actress Robin Wright Penn, who also sat on the festival jury, laughed off rumors that the decision was hotly disputed. "There have been rumors circulating that we were fighting in the room," she told the press conference. "The beauty about loving each other ... [is that] we could disagree, and we still love each other. I felt like we built a consensus among us," she said. "It was like being on "Big Brother," except you could go to the movies," added British screenwriter and fellow juror Hanif Kureishi. "Some of the films are very long," he joked. Elsewhere, Charlotte Gainsbourg won the best actress prize for her shocking turn in Lars von Trier's "Antichrist," featuring scenes of genital mutilation that left audiences stunned. Christolph Waltz won best actor for his role in Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," while Brillante Mendoza secured the best director gong for "Kinatay." The jury prize was shared by Korean auteur Park Chan-Wook's vampire film "Thirst," and Andrea Arnold's "Fish Tank," while the grand prix went to "The Prophet," by director Jacques Audiard.

Haneke also cautioned against believing festival speculation. He recalled that when “Hidden” was shown in 2005, people repeatedly assured him that he would take home the Palme d’Or, but he ultimately did not win.

She characterized “The White Ribbon” as deeply philosophical and said she regarded his filmmaking style and direction as entirely ethical—qualities she wanted the jury to honor.

In her view, the group ultimately reached a shared consensus.

British screenwriter and fellow juror Hanif Kureishi compared the experience to appearing on “Big Brother,” with the difference that the participants were allowed to watch movies. He also joked that some of the films were exceptionally long.

In the other major categories, Charlotte Gainsbourg was named best actress for her disturbing performance in Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist.” The film included scenes of genital mutilation that shocked viewers.

Christolph Waltz received the best actor award for his performance in Quentin Tarantino’s “Inglourious Basterds,” while Brillante Mendoza won best director for “Kinatay.”

# Haneke’s *The White Ribbon* wins Palme d’Or at Cannes

**CANNES, France —** Austrian filmmaker Michael Haneke won the Palme d’Or at the 62nd Cannes Film Festival for *The White Ribbon*, his stark black-and-white drama about repression, cruelty and the roots of authoritarianism in a German village on the eve of the First World War.

Accepting the festival’s highest honor, Haneke thanked his collaborators and paid particular tribute to his wife, Susanne, with whom he has worked for decades. “This is a very happy moment,” he said, adding that the prize belonged to her as well.

The victory crowned a strong Cannes history for Haneke, whose earlier films had already received major festival awards. *The White Ribbon* follows a series of disturbing incidents in a rigid Protestant community, gradually suggesting that violence and humiliation imposed on children can reverberate through an entire society.

Jury president Isabelle Huppert, who starred in Haneke’s *The Piano Teacher*, said the decision reflected the jury’s admiration for the film rather than her previous association with the director. She described *The White Ribbon* as an accomplished work that posed profound questions about guilt, authority and the origins of violence. The Palme decision was reported to have been unanimous.

Juror Robin Wright Penn likewise emphasized the film’s power and precision, saying the panel responded to works that affected its members emotionally rather than attempting to distribute prizes according to politics or national considerations.

Fellow juror Hanif Kureishi said the jury’s discussions had been serious but collegial. He praised Haneke’s film for the force of its ideas and filmmaking, while stressing that the awards represented the panel’s collective judgment among a particularly varied competition slate.

The festival’s Grand Prix went to French director Jacques Audiard’s *A Prophet*, a prison drama about a young inmate’s rise through the criminal hierarchy. Audiard’s film had been widely viewed as one of the chief contenders for the Palme.

Charlotte Gainsbourg received the best-actress award for her emotionally and physically demanding performance in Lars von Trier’s *Antichrist*. Christoph Waltz was named best actor for playing the urbane and menacing Nazi officer Hans Landa in Quentin Tarantino’s *Inglourious Basterds*.

Brillante Mendoza won best director for *Kinatay*, a grim Philippine crime drama. The screenplay prize went to Mei Feng for Lou Ye’s *Spring Fever*.

The Jury Prize was shared by Andrea Arnold’s British coming-of-age drama *Fish Tank* and Park Chan-wook’s Korean vampire film *Thirst*. Veteran French filmmaker Alain Resnais received an exceptional prize recognizing both *Wild Grass* and his body of work.

Among the festival’s other major honors, Warwick Thornton’s Australian drama *Samson and Delilah* won the Caméra d’Or for best first feature. Portuguese director João Salaviza received the Short Film Palme d’Or for *Arena*.

### Major 2009 Cannes award winners

- **Palme d’Or:** *The White Ribbon*, Michael Haneke  
- **Grand Prix:** *A Prophet*, Jacques Audiard  
- **Best Director:** Brillante Mendoza, *Kinatay*  
- **Best Actress:** Charlotte Gainsbourg, *Antichrist*  
- **Best Actor:** Christoph Waltz, *Inglourious Basterds*  
- **Best Screenplay:** Mei Feng, *Spring Fever*  
- **Jury Prize:** *Fish Tank*, Andrea Arnold, and *Thirst*, Park Chan-wook  
- **Exceptional Prize:** Alain Resnais, for *Wild Grass* and his career  
- **Caméra d’Or:** *Samson and Delilah*, Warwick Thornton  
- **Short Film Palme d’Or:** *Arena*, João Salaviza

The 62nd Cannes Film Festival ended on May 24, 2009, with Austrian director Michael Haneke’s **“The White Ribbon”** winning the **Palme d’Or**, the festival’s highest award.

Set in a rigid Protestant village in northern Germany just before World War I, the black-and-white film follows a series of unexplained acts of cruelty and humiliation. Haneke links the village’s authoritarian families, religious repression and harsh treatment of children to the conditions in which political extremism—including the generation that later supported Nazism—could take root.

Jury president **Isabelle Huppert** described the film as an exceptionally powerful and accomplished work of cinema. Although jury deliberations were private, its choice reflected several widely praised qualities:

- Haneke’s austere, meticulously controlled direction  
- Christian Berger’s stark black-and-white cinematography  
- The film’s moral and historical ambition  
- Its refusal to provide easy answers about guilt, violence and collective responsibility  
- Its broader warning about how repression and humiliation can breed fanaticism

The award also marked Haneke’s first Palme d’Or; he would win again in 2012 for *Amour*.

Other principal awards included:

- **Grand Prix:** *A Prophet*, directed by Jacques Audiard  
- **Best Director:** Brillante Mendoza for *Kinatay*  
- **Best Actor:** Christoph Waltz for *Inglourious Basterds*  
- **Best Actress:** Charlotte Gainsbourg for *Antichrist*  
- **Jury Prize:** shared by Andrea Arnold’s *Fish Tank* and Park Chan-wook’s *Thirst*  
- **Best Screenplay:** Mei Feng for *Spring Fever*

Thus, the festival concluded by honoring a film the jury viewed not merely as a period drama, but as a formally rigorous and disturbing examination of the social roots of violence and authoritarianism.

# Cannes closes with honors for “Antichrist,” “Inglourious Basterds” and “The Prophet”

**CANNES, France — May 24, 2009** — The Cannes Film Festival ended with a widely distributed set of awards Sunday, recognizing films ranging from Michael Haneke’s austere period drama *The White Ribbon* to Quentin Tarantino’s exuberant World War II fantasy *Inglourious Basterds*.

Haneke received the festival’s top prize, the **Palme d’Or**, for *The White Ribbon*, a black-and-white drama about disturbing events in a German village on the eve of World War I. Jury president Isabelle Huppert announced the honor at the closing ceremony, bringing the 62nd edition of the festival to an end.

The **Grand Prix**, Cannes’ second-highest award, went to Jacques Audiard’s prison drama *A Prophet*, also known internationally as *The Prophet*. The French film follows a young inmate who learns to survive—and gain power—inside a violent prison hierarchy. It had been considered one of the strongest contenders for the Palme d’Or after receiving an enthusiastic reception during the festival.

Several of Cannes’ most intensely debated films also secured major acting and directing prizes.

Charlotte Gainsbourg was named **best actress** for Lars von Trier’s *Antichrist*. The graphic psychological horror film, co-starring Willem Dafoe, divided audiences with its depictions of grief, sexuality and violence. Gainsbourg’s physically and emotionally demanding performance, however, earned recognition from the jury even as the film itself became one of the festival’s biggest controversies.

Christoph Waltz won **best actor** for his portrayal of the charming but terrifying Nazi officer Col. Hans Landa in Tarantino’s *Inglourious Basterds*. Waltz’s multilingual performance emerged as one of the most celebrated elements of the sprawling revenge fantasy, which stars Brad Pitt as the leader of a group of Jewish American soldiers hunting Nazis in occupied France.

The **best director** prize went to Filipino filmmaker Brillante Mendoza for *Kinatay*. The uncompromising thriller follows a young police academy student drawn into a brutal criminal operation. Its grim subject matter and unflinching style prompted sharply divided reactions, making Mendoza’s victory one of the ceremony’s more striking results.

The jury awarded its **Jury Prize jointly** to two films: Andrea Arnold’s *Fish Tank* and Park Chan-wook’s *Thirst*.  

*Fish Tank*, a British social-realist drama, centers on a volatile teenage girl whose life becomes increasingly complicated when her mother brings home a new boyfriend. *Thirst*, from the South Korean director of *Oldboy*, reworks vampire mythology through the story of a priest transformed after taking part in a medical experiment. The shared award reflected the range of the competition, pairing Arnold’s intimate coming-of-age story with Park’s stylized mixture of horror, romance and dark comedy.

The **best screenplay** award went to Chinese writer Mei Feng for Lou Ye’s *Spring Fever*. Cannes also presented a special festival prize to veteran French director Alain Resnais, whose *Wild Grass* screened in competition.

Warwick Thornton’s Australian drama *Samson and Delilah* received the **Caméra d’Or**, which honors the best first feature shown across Cannes’ official selections. Portuguese filmmaker João Salaviza won the short-film Palme d’Or for *Arena*.

The ceremony capped a festival marked by unusually polarizing entries. *Antichrist* provoked outrage and fascination, *Kinatay* tested viewers with its bleak violence, and *Inglourious Basterds* brought Hollywood spectacle and star power to the Croisette. At the same time, *Fish Tank*, *Thirst* and *The Prophet* strengthened their international profiles with major jury recognition.

Although *The White Ribbon* ultimately claimed the Palme d’Or, the evening’s awards were spread among filmmakers from across Europe and Asia, leaving Cannes with no single dominant winner—and several films positioned to remain in the conversation long after the festival lights went down.

## Haneke’s stark “White Ribbon” takes Cannes’ top prize

**CANNES, France** — Austrian filmmaker Michael Haneke capped his fifth appearance in the race for the Palme d’Or by winning the Cannes Film Festival’s highest honor for **“The White Ribbon,”** a chilling black-and-white portrait of repression and violence in a German village on the eve of World War I.

Technically, Cannes does not announce Palme d’Or “nominations”; the film was Haneke’s fifth selected for the main competition, following **“Funny Games,” “Code Unknown,” “The Piano Teacher”** and **“Caché.”**

Haneke, already a multiple Cannes laureate, thanked jury president Isabelle Huppert and her panel for what he called the courage to honor such an austere film. Huppert described the jury’s decision as unanimous, while fellow jurors praised the movie’s formal control and its unsettling examination of how authoritarianism can take root in families and communities.

The win completed a strong Cannes history for Haneke: **“The Piano Teacher”** had earned the 2001 Grand Prix, along with acting prizes for Isabelle Huppert and Benoît Magimel, while **“Caché”** brought him the 2005 directing award.

### Principal prizes at the 62nd Cannes Film Festival

- **Palme d’Or:** *The White Ribbon* — Michael Haneke  
- **Grand Prix:** *A Prophet* — Jacques Audiard  
- **Best Director:** Brillante Mendoza — *Kinatay*  
- **Jury Prize, shared:**  
  - *Fish Tank* — Andrea Arnold  
  - *Thirst* — Park Chan-wook  
- **Best Actor:** Christoph Waltz — *Inglourious Basterds*  
- **Best Actress:** Charlotte Gainsbourg — *Antichrist*  
- **Best Screenplay:** Mei Feng — *Spring Fever*  
- **Special Jury Prize:** Alain Resnais, for *Wild Grass* and his body of work  
- **Caméra d’Or, best first feature:** *Samson and Delilah* — Warwick Thornton  
- **Short Film Palme d’Or:** *Arena* — João Salaviza  

### Other major Cannes honors

- **Un Certain Regard Prize:** *Dogtooth* — Yorgos Lanthimos  
- **Un Certain Regard Jury Prize:** *Police, Adjective* — Corneliu Porumboiu  
- **Un Certain Regard Special Prize:** *No One Knows About Persian Cats* — Bahman Ghobadi  

The ceremony also delivered one of the festival’s most popular acting victories to Waltz, whose multilingual turn as Nazi officer Hans Landa became the breakout performance of Quentin Tarantino’s **“Inglourious Basterds.”** Gainsbourg’s prize for Lars von Trier’s divisive **“Antichrist,”** meanwhile, underlined a jury willing to reward some of the competition’s most provocative work.

But the night belonged to Haneke, whose severe, meticulously composed drama transformed a quiet German village into a disturbing prehistory of the violence that would engulf Europe.
